lesson.title: Depression, Resentment, and the Rise of Fascism in Europe
lesson.summary: Economic collapse and lingering bitterness over World War One's peace settlement created fertile ground across Europe for fascist movements promising order, national pride, and strong leadership.
lesson.body:
The Treaty of Versailles, which ended World War One in 1919, imposed harsh terms on Germany: a clause assigning Germany blame for the war, heavy reparations payments, loss of territory, and strict limits on its military. Many Germans across the political spectrum viewed the treaty not as a fair peace but as a humiliating imposition, and that resentment undermined public trust in the new democratic Weimar Republic that had to enforce the treaty's terms.

The global economic collapse that began in 1929 hit Europe especially hard. Germany, still recovering from the hyperinflation of 1923 and dependent on American loans that dried up once the Depression struck, saw unemployment climb past 6 million by 1932. Widespread desperation made radical political solutions on both the far left and far right increasingly appealing to voters who felt the existing democratic system could not fix the crisis.

Italy offered an earlier preview of this pattern. Benito Mussolini built the Fascist movement out of postwar disillusionment and economic instability, marched on Rome in October 1922, and was appointed prime minister soon after. Fascism promised national rebirth and order, and it blamed liberal democracy and communism alike for national weakness and decline.

Across much of Europe through the 1920s and 1930s, similar authoritarian and fascist movements gained ground by exploiting fears of economic collapse, communism, and national humiliation. This combination of resentment over Versailles and desperation from the Depression created the conditions in which Adolf Hitler would soon rise to power in Germany.
